video_title: Why gRPC Exists: Contract First RPC for Internal Services
core_insight: gRPC solves internal service-to-service efficiency and contract safety via a single proto contract, codegen, HTTP/2 and protobuf; it is not a browser-facing API.

scenes.voice: Why does a team with 50+ internal services move away from REST/JSON? The pain isn't the idea of HTTP, it's the cost at scale.
scenes.visual: Title card with 50+ service icons, REST/JSON label, latency and payload icons rising.

scenes.voice: Every request pays for text parsing and large payloads. HTTP/1.1 forces one TCP connection per request or complex pooling. There's no standard for bidirectional streaming, and the schema is implicit so breaking changes show up at runtime.
scenes.visual: Split screen: JSON text parsing vs binary protobuf, HTTP/1.1 serial connections vs HTTP/2 multiplex.
scenes.on_screen_text: Parsing cost, connection limits, no streaming standard

scenes.voice: You also need the same contract enforced across Go, Java, Python, TypeScript. The real problem is low latency, efficient wire format, and a single source of truth for the API contract that can generate clients and servers.
scenes.visual: Polyglot services with mismatched types, red warning on breaking change.

scenes.voice: The obvious fix is REST over HTTP/2 with JSON. That helps connections but you still pay text overhead and you still have no enforced schema. The constraint is you need compile-time types and a language-neutral contract.
scenes.visual: Reasonable approach arrow to failure: still JSON, still implicit schema.

scenes.voice: gRPC is contract-first RPC over HTTP/2. You write the API once in .proto, codegen produces strongly typed stubs for each language, and the runtime runs over HTTP/2 with binary protobuf. That's the decision.
scenes.visual: Mermaid flowchart showing client to codegen to stubs to HTTP/2 + protobuf to service.
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    Client[Service A] -->|proto contract| Codegen
    Codegen --> ClientStub
    Codegen --> ServerStub
    ServerStub -->|HTTP/2 + protobuf| Service B
    Service B -->|HTTP/2 + protobuf| Service A

scenes.voice: What you gain is multiplexed streams on one TCP connection, header compression, flow control, 3 to 10x smaller payloads, and early breaking-change detection at compile time. Streaming becomes first class for telemetry, chat, inference.
scenes.visual: Metrics rising down: latency down, bytes down, connections down; streaming arrows.

scenes.voice: What you sacrifice is human readability and browser friendliness. Binary protobuf is hard to debug without tools, HTTP/2 can be blocked by proxies, and you need schema discipline and contract testing to avoid version skew.
scenes.visual: Curl failing on binary, proxy blocking HTTP/2, version skew warning.

scenes.voice: Mental model: use gRPC for internal service mesh where throughput and type safety matter, keep REST/JSON at the public edge via a gateway. The value is the proto contract plus codegen, HTTP/2 and protobuf are enablers.
scenes.visual: Edge gateway translating REST to gRPC, internal mesh labeled gRPC.

mental_model: Think Problem → Constraints → Options → Trade-offs → Decision. For service-to-service: if you need low latency, efficient bytes, streaming, and polyglot type safety, choose contract-first RPC with proto + codegen over HTTP/2. If you need browser or human debuggability, keep REST at the edge.
final_takeaway: gRPC is for internal machine-to-machine efficiency and contract safety, not a REST replacement for the web.
